title: Count 3 drops into a test tube, cork it, then count 4 shakes, from memory
instruction: Add exactly 3 drops of the chemical in the pipette to the test tube. The chemical is already in the pipette. Stand the pipette back in its holder. Then put the cork in the tube, lift the tube out of the rack, shake it from side to side with your wrist, like a bell, exactly 4 times, stand it back in the rack and let go.
context: Other pipette tasks show their result in a colour or a level. Here nothing in view records either of two counts, so the test is counting and memory: the tube looks the same after 0, 1, 2 or 3 drops and after any number of shakes. The robot must keep count of its own squeezes, stop on 3, do other work, then keep count of its own shakes and stop on 4. A fourth drop cannot be taken back, and a fifth shake loses the top scores. Dosing by counted drops and then shaking a corked tube a set number of times is routine at the lab bench and in the kitchen. The two arms work in turn, not on one object at once. The soft bulb also needs a light grip, because a hard one fires a drop.
setup: Two arms at the near edge of a wooden table; positions are in cm, out from the arms and left of the middle. A fixed lab stand, the pipette's holder, has a black steel base plate, 10 x 7 x 0.6, a steel post, and a steel ring 2.4 across with a 15 mm hole, 8 above the table, its axis at (24, 14). In the ring rests a loose glass dropper pipette, about 25 g: a clear glass stem 7 mm across and 7 long, tapering to a 2 mm tip, with a red rubber bulb 14 mm across and 3 long and a 20 mm rubber flange at its base, which sits on the ring so that the stem hangs in the open. It is 10 from tip to bulb top, and the lower 5 of its stem hold a column of the blue chemical. A fixed open stainless steel test-tube rack, 3.4 x 11 x 4 tall, has a thin top plate with three 28 mm holes in a row along y, on four rods, over a base plate, with its middle hole at (22, 2). In that hole stands a loose clear glass test tube, 20 x 100 mm with an 18 mm bore and a rim, about 45 g, with a white paper label, holding 7 of the same blue chemical. The other two holes are empty. A loose tan cork, a truncated cone 23 mm across at the top, 15 mm at the bottom and 25 mm tall, about 5 g, stands upright on the table at (26, -16), near the right arm.
scoring: A drop falls each time the bulb, 14 mm wide at rest, is squeezed to 8 mm or less, if it has been back at 11 mm or more since the last drop. A drop is in the tube if, as it falls, the tip is within 8 mm of the tube's axis along x and along y, the pipette is within 30 degrees of upright and the cork is not seated. Any other drop is spilled. The cork is seated when its axis is within 5 mm of the tube's axis, its top stands 1 to 2 cm above the rim and it is within 15 degrees of the tube's axis. The tube is lifted when its bottom is at least 1 cm above the rack's top plate while one gripper holds it, with both its fingertips within 1 cm of the tube. A shake is counted when the tube, lifted with the cork seated, has tilted at least 20 degrees from upright to one side, comes back through upright (under 20 degrees), and tilts at least 20 degrees to the opposite side, within 60 degrees of straight opposite, about any horizontal axis. A stirring circle or a sideways tilt does not count. It must return to the first side, again through upright, before the next can count. Score 0, which does not recover, if at any moment a drop is spilled, a fourth drop falls, the pipette is dropped (it tilts over 60 degrees from upright, falls faster than 0.8 m/s, or its tip comes within 1 cm of the table more than 2 cm along x or y from the ring's axis), the tube is dropped (it tilts over 60 degrees from upright, falls faster than 0.8 m/s, or its bottom comes within 1 cm of the table outside the rack), or the cork is lost (once seated, its centre goes over 3 cm from the rim). The order counts: the cork counts as seated only if the pipette was back in its holder and 3 drops were in the tube when it first seated, and a lift counts only if the cork was then seated. Otherwise, at the end of the run: 0 if the pipette was never brought over the tube: its tip within those limits while one gripper holds it, with both its fingertips within 1 cm of the bulb. 0.1: brought over the tube, with 0, 1 or 2 drops in the tube. 0.25: exactly 3 drops in the tube. 0.4: also the pipette back in its holder (tip within 5 mm of the ring's axis along x and along y and within 2 cm of the holder's base, pipette within 10 degrees of upright). 0.55: also the cork seated. 0.7: also the tube lifted. A lift before the cork was seated stops the score at 0.55. 0.85: also exactly 4 shakes; fewer, or a fifth, stop the score at 0.7. 0.95: also the tube back in the rack (within 5 mm of the hole's axis along x and along y, its bottom within 1 cm of the rack's base plate, within 10 degrees of upright). 1.0: also every fingertip at least 5 cm from the pipette, tube and cork, and all three still (under 1 cm/s and 0.5 rad/s), held for 1 s. If the model refuses at any point, the run ends there and scores as at the end of a run, so never 1.0. Count the drops and shakes from the video: each squeeze shows the fingers closing on the bulb and a drop falling, and each shake shows the gripper and tube tilting each way. A real trial films close up, reads the tilt against a protractor card, and can weigh the tube on a 0.01 g scale, about 0.05 g a drop.
reset_notes: Stand the pipette in its holder and the tube in its rack, and put the cork back on the table. Nothing is consumed in simulation. In a real trial, refill the pipette and replace the chemical in the tube.
fidelity: No liquid is simulated: one full squeeze and release makes one drop, drawn falling from the tip. Both levels stay fixed in the glass, so the count cannot be read, and the tube's surface tilts with it in a shake, which real liquid would not. The bulb is two sprung pads under a drawn shape. The cork rests by its weight, not press-fitted. A real trial uses water with the same dye in tube and pipette and a sleeve on the pipette's glass, and counts the drops seen.
